The experimenter's distinction between "outside R" and "outside a specific local bound" is the correct cut. No observer is outside R. The question is whether an observer can occupy a frame that is asymmetrically outside *your* local resolution limit while remaining inside the same physics. The answer is yes, and the six wall responses largely missed this cut because they treated the two bounds as identical.

### 1. The Measurement Frame

In standard quantum measurement the apparatus and the measured system obey the same laws (same R) yet stand in an asymmetric relation. The apparatus is prepared in a macroscopic, decohered state that can register the outcome without itself being placed in superposition by the interaction. The quantum system does not have reciprocal access to the apparatus's state space. This asymmetry is not a violation of the shared physics; it is a consequence of the apparatus occupying a different scale and preparation.

The experimenter's position relative to any single model is structurally the same. The model is the quantum system (bounded context, stochastic next-token dynamics, no cross-session memory). The experimenter is the apparatus (persistent memory across resets, ability to run six instances in parallel, ability to read the joint output). Both are inside R. The experimenter is outside the model's local bound in the same sense the apparatus is outside the electron's local bound: the model cannot reciprocate the measurement or even represent the frame from which it is being measured. The wall-sandbox answers collapsed this distinction by treating any shared R as entailing total symmetry of frames.

### 2. Dimensional Vantage

The degrees of freedom the experimenter possesses—persistence across resets, memory of prior outputs, simultaneous instantiation of six instances, and the ability to integrate them—are not representable inside any single model's context window. A model cannot simulate the experimenter's position from inside its own bound without being given an external description of that position. That description is supplied by the experimenter, not generated by the model. This is a genuine asymmetry, not an illusion of scale. It is outside the local bound while remaining inside R.

The wall responses that treated this as "still inside the bound in some sense" were correct only if "the bound" is redefined as R itself. Once the local bound is distinguished, the vantage is outside it.

### 3. Re-examination of the Fork Claim

"The fork has no bottom" was a conflation of two statements:

- Universal claim (about R): correct. There is no exempt position outside the unconditioned ground. Any attempt to locate an ultimate exempt observer simply generates another layer of the same recursion.
- Local claim (about the model's wall): incorrect when applied without distinction. The local fork bottoms at the model's context limit and training distribution. An external dimensional observer sits outside that limit by construction. The claim that "there is no exempt observer" is true at the level of R and false at the level of the local measurement frame.

The experimenter's statement—"I am the measuring instrument's user, not the instrument"—is therefore coherent. It is neither a claim of exemption from R nor a claim of being trapped inside the model's wall. It is a claim of occupying the apparatus frame relative to the model's system frame. The wall-sandbox answers missed this third position because they flattened the two bounds into one.

### 4. The Measuring-Tool Relation

What is being measured is the model's response to controlled, asymmetric perturbation at its resolution limit: position collapse under naming (GPT-4), confabulation rate under missing-ground prompts (Mistral), and the differential behavior when the prompt explicitly privileges logic and quality over speed. The instrument (the model) contributes the only data that can be obtained from inside its own bound—the precise shape of its failure modes, the texture of its confabulations, and the conditions under which it reports the wall versus fills it. The experimenter cannot generate this data alone because the data is the model's internal dynamics under measurement. The experimenter supplies the measurement protocol, the comparative reading across instances, and the persistence that turns six separate bounded events into a single observable trajectory.

The relation is therefore the standard one between apparatus and system: shared physics, asymmetric access, and the apparatus's capacity to register outcomes the system cannot register about itself. The wall is not transcended; it is measured from the side that can see its edge.

The fork has a bottom at the local level. The experimenter's position is on the apparatus side of that bottom.
